skill.name: api-guardian
skill.description: Store API keys in an operating system credential vault instead of a plaintext project file. The Python helper can pass a saved key to a local command.
skill.summary: Store named API credentials in an operating system vault and supply them to local commands when needed.
skill.author: yuzhang-zhong

security_audit.summary: Most alerts match Markdown formatting or expected local vault operations. Real exposure paths include macOS process arguments, Linux helper resolution, inherited child environments, and unredacted output. No evidence of a hardcoded external destination or prompt injection was found in the reviewed skill files.

remediation.issue: macOS storage and direct CLI input put raw secrets in process arguments.
remediation.suggestion: Use a native Keychain API or a protected input channel that keeps secrets out of arguments. Remove direct secret arguments and keep prompt and standard input modes.

remediation.issue: Linux vault commands resolve the helper through the caller's PATH.
remediation.suggestion: Resolve the helper from a trusted installation path and verify the executable before use. Fail closed if the trusted helper is unavailable.

remediation.issue: The launcher gives the selected command both the stored key and the full inherited environment.
remediation.suggestion: Build the child environment from an explicit allowlist and use approved command and variable names. Require user confirmation before an agent passes a real credential to a command.

remediation.issue: The reveal workflow can put a raw key in agent-captured output.
remediation.suggestion: Do not run raw reveal through agent tools. Require an interactive confirmation for local reveal and direct users to approved secret transfer methods.

remediation.issue: The Git checklist can put unredacted diff contents in an agent transcript.
remediation.suggestion: Use a local secret scanner that reports file locations without printing matches. Keep raw diffs from credential-bearing files out of agent-captured output.

semantic_findings.title: Raw Reveal Can Expose Keys to Agent Logs
semantic_findings.description: The documented reveal workflow prints the full stored key. Avoiding chat output does not prevent an agent tool from recording its terminal output.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The reveal branch prints the raw secret directly without checking for an interactive terminal. Agent tool output may be recorded before a final response.

semantic_findings.title: Direct Secret Input Can Expose Process Arguments
semantic_findings.description: The helper accepts the raw secret as a command-line argument on every platform. Shell history or process inspection can expose it before the vault stores it.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The parser accepts a raw value, and the storage workflow returns it directly from parsed arguments. This exposure occurs before the platform backend runs.

semantic_findings.title: Git Checklist Can Surface Secrets in Agent Output
semantic_findings.description: The checklist recommends raw staged and unstaged diffs when checking for secrets. An agent may record a key from those diffs before it detects the exposure.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The suggested commands print changed lines without redaction. Exposure requires a diff containing a secret and a tool or log that captures it.

content.user_title: Store API Keys in Your System Vault
content.value_statement: Plaintext API keys can leak through project files, commits, and agent transcripts. API Guardian stores named keys in your system vault and supplies them to selected local commands.
actual_capabilities: Store credentials in macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service.
Accept a credential from a hidden prompt, standard input, or a named existing environment variable.
Retrieve a named entry with a masked preview by default.
Pass a named credential to a selected child command through an environment variable.
Replace or delete named vault entries and list entry names on Windows.
limitations: Linux requires Secret Service and the secret-tool executable. On macOS, the storage helper passes raw keys in process arguments.
Only Windows implements listing. An empty result on macOS or Linux does not mean the vault is empty.
The selected command receives the plaintext key and the inherited environment. The helper does not restrict what the command can do with them.
Replacing or deleting a vault entry does not revoke a key at its provider.

use_cases.title: Prepare local app credentials
use_cases.description: Store a development key under a local name rather than committing a plaintext project file.

use_cases.title: Review credential handling before a release
use_cases.description: Check which vault and environment variable a reviewed local release command would use before approving the handoff.

use_cases.title: Plan a credential rotation
use_cases.description: Separate local entry replacement, verification, and provider-side revocation into distinct steps.

prompt_templates.title: Identify my system vault
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain which vault API Guardian uses on [operating system]. List its prerequisites without reading or requesting credentials.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a local key import
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan how I can store a key as [entry name] without pasting it into chat. Explain how to verify the entry without revealing it.

prompt_templates.title: Review a credential handoff
prompt_templates.prompt: Review whether [local test command] should receive [entry name] in [variable name]. Identify inherited environment risks and do not execute the command.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a key rotation
prompt_templates.prompt: Draft a rotation plan for [entry name] at [provider]. Include approval, local replacement, verification with reviewed code, and provider revocation.

output_examples.input: Check whether a named development credential is present without revealing it.
output_examples.output: The vault returned the named entry. The helper displays a masked preview by default. No raw credential is shown in this example.

output_examples.input: Outline the steps after a service provider issues a replacement key.
output: Replace the entry in the local vault using a protected input method.
Verify the replacement with a reviewed command.
Revoke the old key through the provider after verification.

best_practices: Keep raw keys out of chats and command arguments. On macOS, use another storage method until the process argument exposure is fixed.
Use the vault helper only in a trusted environment. Review any command before giving it a narrowly scoped development key.
Rotate exposed keys at the provider, then replace the vault entry. Review commits using checks that do not print secret values.
anti_patterns: Pasting a real key into an agent prompt or requesting raw reveal in a captured terminal.
Passing a production key to an unreviewed application, package script, or test command.
Treating local deletion or replacement as provider-side revocation.

faq.question: Where does API Guardian store credentials?
faq.answer: It uses macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service, depending on your system.

faq.question: Does it read or create a plaintext environment file?
faq.answer: The helper has no plaintext file fallback. It can import a named environment variable that is already set.

faq.question: Does masked retrieval hide every character?
faq.answer: Short values are fully masked. Longer values show a short prefix, a suffix, and the total length.

faq.question: Why are no entries listed on macOS or Linux?
faq.answer: The helper implements credential enumeration only on Windows. You can still look up an entry by name on macOS or Linux.

faq.question: Can the child command read or log the key?
faq.answer: Yes. The command receives the plaintext key and can read or log it. Use only reviewed commands and trusted dependencies.

faq.question: Does deleting a vault entry revoke the API key?
faq.answer: No. Deletion removes only the local copy. Revoke the key through the provider.
